text: An ADR explains one decision in words. A diagram is usually the first thing a new engineer or outside reviewer looks at to understand the shape of a system before reading any of the decisions behind it. That only works if the diagram follows notation the reader already recognizes, which is what this lesson is actually about.

Simon Brown's C4 model gives you four nested levels. Context is the whole system as one box, showing who or what talks to it -- the level you'd show a non-technical stakeholder. Container breaks it into its major deployable pieces, and this is where most enterprise architecture documentation should actually live: detailed enough to be useful, stable enough not to need constant redrawing. Component and Code go deeper than a cross-team review usually needs.

Two notational conventions matter more than any specific shape library. A trust boundary is a dashed rectangle around a zone sharing one level of trust -- a VNet, an account, a subnet behind a firewall. Anything a data-flow arrow crosses out of a boundary is worth a reviewer's attention. And every arrow should be labeled with what's actually moving and how -- HTTPS, gRPC, JDBC -- pointed in the real direction, not just drawn as a connecting line.

Pick one official icon set per diagram, Azure or AWS, and don't mix it with ad-hoc boxes. Keep one zoom level per diagram too -- don't drop one deeply detailed VM into an otherwise Container-level view. Mixing either one forces a reader to guess whether a visual difference means something or is just inconsistency, and that guesswork is exactly what breaks a diagram once it has to serve someone who wasn't in the room when it was drawn.

With three engineers who built the system together, an inconsistent diagram still works because everyone fills in the gaps from memory. That stops being true the moment the team doubles. Next lesson covers the other half of staying usable: keeping both the ADRs and the diagrams from quietly going stale as the real infrastructure keeps changing underneath them.
